vectors.reason: ENISA names no origin; the text implies parameters are changed through commands from the operator's ground system (deliberate or incorrect).
Weak: 'test procedures' implies the assembly and test environment, which the supplier/integrator origin attaches to; ENISA does not say so.

rows.reason: Using an existing function as designed is not what ENISA describes; it states changed parameters.
ENISA names parameter changes and restarts, not a forced operating state or mode.

rows.sparta_quote: deliberate alteration of authoritative, non-executable settings or structured artifacts that govern spacecraft behavior
rows.reason: Altering satellite parameters is the configuration manipulation ENISA names.
Altering data values, not parameters or settings, is the data-modification threat TR39.
Changing how commands or data move is not described.
Replacing code or firmware is TR42; ENISA's text is about parameters and procedures.
Exhausting resources is TR51; infinite restarts here come from watchdog/RTOS tampering.
Clock or synchronisation shifts are not described.
Ground compromise in general is not stated; the valid-command route (IA-0007.02) is the closer fit to parameter changes.
Manipulating the update pipeline is TR46's injection into updates; in TR57 update tampering is only a later consequence of parameter changes, not the way in.
Weak inference: a deliberate or mistaken parameter change from the mission's own ground system is commanded through valid ground commands, which is what this technique describes.
rows.sparta_quote: modifying rate/size limits or command queues

rows.reason: Backup ground station access is not described.
Safe-mode timing is not described.

rows.sparta_quote: The attacker alters live or persistent data that the spacecraft uses to make decisions and route work
rows.reason: Modify On-Board Values is the parameter modification ENISA describes.

rows.sparta_quote: Threat actors target these parameters and associated tables to skew execution order and timing
rows.reason: Real-time scheduling parameters are RTOS components, named by ENISA.

rows.enisa_quote: result in infinite restarts of the satellite
rows.sparta_quote: forcing repeated resets at tactically chosen moments
rows.reason: Manipulating the watchdog yields the repeated resets ENISA states.
rows.role_reason: Execution technique that is the stated outcome: ENISA's 'infinite restarts' is the repeated watchdog-forced reset itself.

rows.sparta_quote: compromised laptops or transient cyber assets push images and tables
rows.reason: Weak inference from 'test procedures': ATLO test tooling pushes images and tables into the flight hardware, a place where parameters and test procedures are modified.
Inserting malicious code or configuration during manufacturing is TR55's supply-chain compromise; the ENISA text is about changed parameters.
Poisoned dependencies and development tools are TR55's case; no dependency is named.
Subverted software delivery is TR55; ENISA's parameters are values, not delivered software.
Hardware tampering before delivery is TR55; parameters are not hardware.
Compromise of a software-defined radio is not described; the CDHS is the named asset.
Crosslink access from a neighbour satellite is not described.
A secondary command channel is not described.
A backup RF receive path is not described.
Rendezvous and proximity operations are not described.
Emanation capture does not modify parameters.
Docked-vehicle access is not described.
Grappling is not described.
A hosted-payload doorway is not described; the named asset is the CDHS.
An external transmitter is not named; parameter changes are described as deliberate or incorrect, i.e. by someone with access.
A rogue ground station is not described.
A rogue spacecraft is not described.
Counterspace platforms are not described.
Trusted-relationship access is not described.
Collaborator access is not described.
Vendor remote access is not described.
User-segment access is not described.
Malicious peripherals or removable media are TR20; no such device is named here.
Pivot from a host spacecraft into a hosted payload is not described.
Pivoting through a hosted-payload boundary is not described.
Hopping across a crosslink is not described.
